title: Pointwise local upper bound for extended Taylor Hilbert functions
statement:
Let $k$ be a characteristic-zero field, $U$ a smooth affine finite-type $k$-scheme with etale coordinates $t_1,\ldots,t_d$, and $X\hookrightarrow U$ a closed subscheme [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] [def-weil-etale-morphism] [def-weil-closed-immersion]. For each $y\in U$ let $K_y\subset\kappa(y)[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]]$ be the extension of the ideal of $X$ under the centered Taylor map, after residue-field base change and completion at the diagonal point [def-weil-residue-field] [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Define
$$H_y(q)=\dim_{\kappa(y)}\kappa(y)[[T]]/(K_y+(T)^{q+1}).$$
For $y\notin X$ this is the zero function. Fix $a\in X$ and suppose on an affine neighbourhood $U_0$ the set $\mathcal H=\{H_y:y\in U_0\}$ is finite, and for each $q$ the function $y\mapsto H_y(q)$ is the fibre dimension of a finite module over $\mathcal O(U_0)$. Then there is an open neighbourhood $V\subset U_0$ of $a$ such that
$$\forall y\in V\ \forall q\ge0,\qquad H_y(q)\le H_a(q).$$
In particular the inequality holds in lexicographic order. Each finite module in this assertion has a finite presentation. Its locus of fibre dimension at most a specified integer is the union of the opens where a corresponding presentation-matrix minor is nonzero; these conditions therefore define the required open sets by finite regular matrices.
More explicitly, for every $h\in\mathcal H$ which fails $h\le H_a$ pointwise, choose one degree $q_h$ with $h(q_h)>H_a(q_h)$. One may take $V$ to be the intersection of the finitely many conditions $H_y(q_h)\le H_a(q_h)$, allowing $V=U_0$ if there are none. One may simultaneously impose finitely many further degree bounds, including degrees distinguishing every pair of functions in $\mathcal H$. No intersection over all natural numbers is required.
The finite-value and finite-module hypotheses hold for these Taylor functions on a sufficiently small $U_0$, using the principal-parts modules of the affine scheme $X$: if $A=\mathcal O(X)$ and $J=\ker(A\otimes_k A\to A)$, the module is $(A\otimes_k A)/J^{q+1}$, extended as an $\mathcal O(U_0)$-module via the closed immersion. The statement includes nonclosed $a,y$ with the full $d$ Taylor variables and includes $X=U$ and $d=0$.

proof.text: Put $R=\mathcal O(U_0)$ and choose finite $R$-modules $M_q$ realizing the stipulated fibre dimensions. Since $U\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is of finite type, hence locally of finite type, and $U_0\subseteq U$ is an affine open, [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs] (with $V=\operatorname{Spec}k$) shows that $R$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra. Thus $R$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian], since every ideal of the field $k$ is either zero or the whole field. By [lem-sc-noetherian-finite-module-finite-presentation] each $M_q$ is finitely presented. In the sense of [def-sc-finitely-presented-module], choose $R^{u_q}\xrightarrow{B_q}R^{v_q}\to M_q\to0$.

proof.text: For $y\in U_0$ put $L=\kappa(y)$. Tensor right exactness gives $L^{u_q}\xrightarrow{B_q(y)}L^{v_q}\to M_q\otimes_RL\to0$. Thus the fibre is the quotient by the column span of $B_q(y)$, and the quotient-dimension identity gives $H_y(q)+\operatorname{rank}B_q(y)=v_q$. Consequently, for $0\le b<v_q$, $H_y(q)\le b$ if and only if some $(v_q-b)$-minor of $B_q(y)$ is nonzero. Here a nonzero $r$-minor forces rank at least $r$ by the largest-minor characterization, and conversely if the rank $\rho$ is at least $r$ a nonzero $\rho$-minor exists; Laplace expansion of that determinant along a row shows some $(\rho-1)$-minor of it is nonzero, and descending gives a nonzero $r$-minor. This uses exactly the column-span and largest-nonzero-minor characterizations of rank in [def-weil-matrix-rank].

proof.text: Each such minor is the residue of the determinant $\delta\in R$ of the same submatrix of $B_q$: the determinant is the finite signed sum of permutation products, so it commutes with $R\to\kappa(y)$. This residue is nonzero exactly when $\delta\notin y$. Hence $W(q,b)=\{y:H_y(q)\le b\}$ is the finite union of the basic opens $D(\delta)$ for those minors. For $b<0$ the locus is empty since a vector-space dimension is nonnegative. For $b\ge v_q$ it is all of $U_0$ (use the size-zero minor $1$); an unavailable positive minor gives the empty union. This proves both openness and the asserted finite regular-matrix description, including zero-row and zero-column presentations.

proof.text: Let $\mathcal B=\{h\in\mathcal H:\exists q,\ h(q)>H_a(q)\}$. It is finite. For each $h\in\mathcal B$ choose one witnessing $q_h$ and set $V=\bigcap_{h\in\mathcal B}W(q_h,H_a(q_h))$. These are finitely many open sets containing $a$, so $V$ is an open neighbourhood; the empty intersection is $U_0$. If $y\in V$ had $H_y(q)>H_a(q)$ for some $q$, then $h=H_y$ would lie in $\mathcal B$, whereas membership in its chosen factor gives $h(q_h)\le H_a(q_h)$, a contradiction. Conversely a point satisfying all degree bounds belongs to $V$. Thus the finite intersection equals the full pointwise bounded locus. Pointwise inequality implies lexicographic inequality: for unequal sequences use the least differing index.

proof.text: For a finite set $E$ of additional degrees, intersect also the opens $W(q,H_a(q))$, $q\in E$. They contain $a$, and Step 4 shows they already contain $V$. More generally any finite list $H_y(q)\le b_q$ with $b_q\ge H_a(q)$ can be imposed. For each pair of distinct functions in the finite set $\mathcal H$, choose a degree where they differ; there are finitely many pairs. Taking these degrees as $E$ gives the asserted simultaneous distinguishing tests without an infinite intersection.

proof.text: For the geometric hypotheses, replace $X$ by $X\cap U_0$ and put $A=\mathcal O(X\cap U_0)=R/I$. The diagonal modules $P^q_{A/k}$ of [def-trf-diagonal-jets] are finite, and [lem-trf-jet-diagram-hilbert-control] identifies their residue-field fibre dimensions at every $y\in X$ with the full-$d$-variable Taylor quotients in the statement. Viewed through $R\twoheadrightarrow A$, a finite $A$-module is finite over $R$, with the same generators. Its fibre outside $X$ is zero: choose $f\in I\setminus y$; it annihilates the module but acts invertibly on $\kappa(y)$, so the tensor product vanishes. Also $\tau_y(f)$ has nonzero constant coefficient and is a unit (invert it by the formal geometric series), so $K_y=(1)$ there. Finally the same cited theorem gives locally finitely many Taylor diagrams; its monomial-complement counting formula gives finitely many functions on a sufficiently small affine $U_0$. Thus the hypotheses used in Steps 1--5 hold, with the principal-parts modules extended along the closed immersion. No reducedness or closed-point assumption is used; the unit and zero ideals and $d=0$ are included.
